vignette:
She works the night shift in the emergency department of a large urban hospital, a job she has held for seven years. Three years ago, during her evening shift, a massive gas explosion ripped through a nearby residential building. She was among the first responders. The call came in as a “mass casualty incident,” and within minutes the triage bay was flooded with the wounded, the burned, the dying. She remembers the smell—a thick, sweet-chemical burn mixed with blood and dust. She remembers a young woman, maybe twenty-five, with a piece of rebar through her chest, eyes wide and silent. She remembers holding pressure on a wound that would not stop bleeding, her hands slippery, the patient’s pulse fading under her fingers. She remembers the sound of a child screaming for her mother, and then the quiet when the child stopped.

That night ended, but it did not leave her.

Now, in the present, she moves through her shifts like a ghost. She avoids the trauma bay whenever possible, volunteering for triage or the observation unit instead. The sound of an alarm—any alarm—makes her drop whatever she is holding. The first time it happened, she shattered a tray of syringes. Her coworkers have learned to warn her before they pull the fire alarm for drills. She does not talk about the explosion. When a new colleague asks about the scar on her forearm—a small burn from falling debris she barely noticed that night—she says she cut herself on a broken glass at home.

At night, she does not sleep. She lies in her studio apartment, the television on low, her back to the wall, facing the door. She has checked the gas stove four times before every bedtime for the past year. The nightmares come anyway: the rebar, the child, the smell. Sometimes she wakes up gasping, her hands clenched as if still holding pressure. Her mother calls from overseas every Sunday. She tells her work is fine, stress is normal, she is meeting people. She is not. She has not gone out with friends in eighteen months. She canceled on her cousin’s wedding. She deleted the dating apps. She tells herself she is just tired.

She is tired. She is also afraid—of crowds, of sudden noises, of the way her heart hammers when she hears a siren. She double-checks the emergency exits in every room she enters, counts the steps to the nearest stairwell, scans for heavy objects that could fall. In the hospital cafeteria, she sits with her back to the wall, facing the entrance. She cannot stand the smell of grilled meat. It reminds her of the explosion.

Her patients notice something is off. She is efficient but distant. She avoids eye contact when a patient reminds her of the young woman with the rebar. She once walked out of a trauma code and vomited in the supply closet. Her supervisor has suggested she take leave. She said no. Work is the only place where she feels she has some control, even if it is fragile.

She came to therapy because she is afraid she will make a mistake on the job. She does not say she is afraid of falling apart entirely. She sits on the edge of the chair, her hands folded, her voice flat. She describes her days as a series of tasks she must complete. She has not cried in two years. She has not felt much of anything except the constant low hum of vigilance. When asked what she wants, she shrugs. “I just want to stop checking the stove,” she says. “I want to sleep through the night.” She does not mention the explosion by name. She does not have to. It is in the room with her every moment.
